speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION AND WORK OF SESSION '
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I need hardly say that I am in complete accord with my hon. friend in his desire to have the business of the session conducted as rapidly and efficiently as possible. He may be sure that the government will make every effort in that direction. I regret that I have not the vision of a prophet or a seer and therefore am unable to give my hon. friend direct assurances with respect to all that is going to happen in the course of the session. I shall indicate to him in general terms the course which the government intends to follow, though naturally how the session proceeds will depend, among other things, upon circumstances beyond the control of parliment, to begin with, and, within parliament itself, certainly beyond the control of the government. However, it is gratifying to realize that hon. members of all parties appear to share the hope of the government that the debate on the address will not be prolonged unduly. I have no desire in any way to curtail the right or privilege of any hon. member to speak in any debate, but I do believe that in previous years the debate on the address frequently has run on much too long. Last year it continued for a month or more, and I believe the public deprecated the length of time it took the House of Commons to conclude that debate. If there is general agreement in the view that the address should be voted in short order, I can assure my hon. friend that other legislation is ready now to be taken up immediately the debate is concluded.
As to the general business, if hon. members will look at the speech from the throne they will see that it falls naturally into three parts. The first part refers to the war and the importance of war measures receiving consideration ahead of all others. There can be nothing as important as the winning of the war and making every necessary provision toward that end at as early a date as possible. Then follow the measures that relate to the period of transition between the close of the war and the establishment of peace. The fact that the speech from the throne dwells at some length on these measures, and on others, must not be taken as an indication that the government entertains any belief that the war is going to end suddenly, or soon. The contrary, as I said the other day, is the view of the administration. I believe the war will last much longer than most of us have assumed it would.
However, it is part of the government's obligation to anticipate, so far as possible, situations which may arise in any eventuality. And for that reason we have had already to take carefully into consideration, as did committees of the house at the last session, those situations which will arise once the war is at an end. The first of the new situations would be that arising from the conditions in devastated areas in Europe, conditions in countries which have suffered, and which will experience need of assistance from the united nations, in order that their peoples may be enabled to reestablish themselves.
Simultaneously there will also be the most important work of the demobilization of our own forces, and making provision for their reestablishment in orderly fashion. Certain measures will be necessary in that connection. I might describe these measures as illustrative of what is related to the transitional period.
Then, following that, measures by way of reforms will be required, if the new era is to be an improvement on the old one-and we certainly hope and expect it will be. Many measures of social reform will have to be carefully considered. But they cannot be considered by this House of Commons alone because, as hon. members well know, under our constitution certain obligations are assigned to the federal government, and others to the provincial governments. Close cooperation will be required between provincial and dominion authorities if we are to bring into being a nation-wide programme of social security and human well-being.
I do not wish to discuss a matter which might be the subject of debate, but may I point out that in his amendment my hon. friend opposite has stressed the importance of the dominion in its social and fiscal measures not invading the jurisdiction of the provinces. When my hon. friend, the leader of the C.C.F., was speaking in the debate he said-the speech from the throne indicated a first-rate example of passing the buck from the dominion to the provinces. I leave hon. members to judge for themselves as to just in what position the government is placed when dealing with these matters. I, myself, cannot find any sure path to follow, other than that laid down in the constitution of our country as a guide, and what in the way of cooperation will, we hope, be the attitude of all governments in Canada at this time in seeking to meet situations which will lie ahead of us all.
So, speaking broadly, we find the legislation for this session divided into those three fields, namely that which relates immediately to the prosecution of the war, that which relates to the transitional period, and that relating to

Business of the House-Legislation
social problems which will also follow immediately after the war ends, and in larger measure as we enter the period of peace. The government will seek to introduce its legislation, broadly, on those lines.
The measures we wish to take up first of all are those related to the prosecution of the war. Then, as I have said, we will proceed to those matters arising immediately from the war and in the post-war period, and other measures will follow in due course. I am not laying down a hard and fast line. As hon. members know, there are some subjects, the discussion of which will take a longer time than others. There are some we may wish to discuss immediately, and then allow some time to intervene before renewing discussion on them. There are always miscellaneous measures. They will be interspersed. The government will have to judge in respect of those matters what it thinks will best serve to meet the general need. Broadly, however, I have outlined the position.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) asked if we can have all these measures introduced this week. I do not think he is serious when he prefers a request of that kind. No administration has ever brought down its whole programme within the first five days of the session-unless it was intended that the session should last about that length of time.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION AND WORK OF SESSION '
speechtext: That is not the only reason.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION AND WORK OF SESSION '
speechtext: However, we will keep the house plentifully supplied with legislation, and if hon. members feel they have not had the time necessary to consider certain legislation before debate is opened in the house, they have only to ask that they be given a little time, and it will be afforded. That is what we seek to do. We do not wish to congest the order paper with a large number of measures, but rather it is our desire to bring before the house in an orderly fashion and in accordance with the plans I have indicated first of all the measures which are the most pressing.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION AND WORK OF SESSION '

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION AND WORK OF SESSION '
speechtext:
My hon. friend has his responsibility with respect to the introduction of bills, and I have mine. I should not wish to see measures brought down at other than what I regard as the most appropriate time. The government must be the judge of that.
The next query raised by the leader of the opposition was as to whether we can have all committees appointed this week. May I say to him that that depends on him much more

than on me. It depends on other hon. members and other parties in the house rather than on the government. The complaint has been made that last year a long time elapsed before some of these committees were established. I shall not at this time go over the reasons for that, but I would point out in passing that one of the reasons was that, time and again, when we hoped to be able to proceed with a motion related to the appointment of some committee, we were prevented from so doing by a motion from the other side of the. house, occasioning at different times debate which ran on for some days, and the opportunity to get committees appointed was precluded from day to day and often from week to week.
Then there was a further fact-and this is important-namely, that there was a desire on the part of some hon. members to start debates on the several motions to establish committees. On one or two occasions I was asked to please hold over my motion to constitute a committee-the committee on war expenditures was one-because it was the desire of certain hon. members to have a debate upon the motion.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION AND WORK OF SESSION '
speechtext: Of course the Prime Minister knows why that was.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION AND WORK OF SESSION '
speechtext: I have forgotten it-if I ever did know.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION AND WORK OF SESSION '
speechtext: Well, I can tell him, if he wishes to know.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION AND WORK OF SESSION '
speechtext:
I am no longer interested as it belongs to the past; but what I wish to say now is that- if hon. members are prepared to allow these committees to be constituted without debate, and that is the position they will take with respect to each committee as its appointment is proposed, I would undertake to say that practically all committees will be established this week. As hon. members will have seen, notice appears in Votes and Proceedings of motions for most of committees that remain to be constituted.. If it is the wish of the house-and it would be very helpful in every way if such proved to be so-I believe those committees could be established at once. If there could be an understanding that there would be no debate-no lengthy debate-on the establishment of the committees, I am sure we could forward them in such fashion that practically all standing and select committees would be established this week.
My hon. friend asked if it was the plan of the government to go on with the war appropriation measure, immediately after the conclusion of the debate on the address. That is the intention. As soon as the debate on the

Business oj the House-Legislation
address is concluded the war appropriation resolution, now appearing on the order paper, will be the first item for the consideration of the house, with the possible exception of some routine motion or motion respecting the appointment of further committees. The bill based upon the resolution is ready to be introduced, and it is the intention with respect to the discussion on the bill to follow the same order of procedure as was adopted last year. That is to say, the estimates with respect to the war appropriation resolution will be broken down, as before, and the debate will proceed on the different branches of the service, taking one service at a time.
My hon. friend asked me at what stage of the session the budget would be brought down. I cannot answer that question offhand because that will depend upon how much time is taken up with the other war measures which will be brought forward in succession. Following the war appropriation measure, without a very long delay, there will be brought down a measure with respect to mutual aid, This year this measure will relate to aid in the nature of relief to countries in Europe as well as to war supplies. I would hope that both of these important war measures might be disposed of before the budget is brought down.
In referring to these matters I think I ought to stress the tremendous load that necessarily falls upon the shoulders of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). Most of the measures of defence in a time of war are financial in character and the Minister of Finance will have a heavy load to carry in bringing forward these measures one after another. But he tells me that he feels he is equal to it. If the house will, as it has done before, cooperate with him I think we can have these measures brought along fairly Boon.
There are also the estimates. They will be ready and tabled shortly. The government hopes to get on with the estimates a little more rapidly this year than has been the case in previous years. It is an open question as to whether more progress is made in the end by having one particular measure discussed at considerable length until it is completed or to break up the discussion and take on other measures in the interim. I am inclined to believe that perhaps it is better not to stick too closely to any one measure through every day in the week but rather to vary the programme in some particulars, while holding in the main to getting through a particular measure. We should I think introduce other bills, some of which may be of minor importance, and have discussions on different
subjects so that the discussion on a particular measure may not become too monotonous. The estimates can be taken up on. one or more days in the week and we shall hope to begin with them at an early stage of the session.
The leader of the opposition has asked me what legislation the government intends to introduce other than that mentioned in the speech from the throne. I cannot indicate to him at the moment what further legislation there will be. There is one bill with respect to the disposal of obsolete war materials which will be brought forward and there are other measures I cannot recall at the moment. There may arise a number of measures in the course of the session. At this moment I am not in position to tell my hon. friend what they will be. The speech from the throne does not usually make mention of all intended legislation.
I have been asked whether it is the intention to adjourn parliament while I attend the conference of commonwealth prime ministers. Here again I cannot speak with any degree of certainty because I do not know when this conference will take place. It is likely to be some short time hence, but whether it would be advisable to adjourn will depend, first of all, on the time at which the meeting takes place and, next, on the progress that meanwhile has been made with the different war measures.
I should point out to the house that before very long the government hopes to have a conference between the dominion and the provinces. The government has been ready ever since the last conference with the provinces to have another dominion-provincial conference and we have reason to believe that the provinces now are ready and willing, some of them I understand quite anxious to meet with the federal government in conference to discuss some of the social problems and financial questions that they along with ourselves have had necessarily to consider. It may be that an adjournment would be advisable in connection with a conference of the kind. It might be possible to arrange to have it take place at the time the meeting of prime ministers is taking place in London. However, I cannot say as to that at the moment or whether it will be necessary or advisable to have an adjournment at the time. I do say, however, that the fact that we are faced with the possibility of an adjournment gives an additional reason why this house should in the interval seek to make all the progress it possibly can with the war measures.
The last question my hon. friend asked was whether there were any other general sessional

Business oj the House-Legislation
plans which the Prime Minister would care to disclose to the house. I have not any in in mind at the moment. If any should develop I shall be glad to acquaint my hon. friend with them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think all hon. members wish to expedite the business of the house. During the past several sessions, however, there have been no private members' days, and opportunities are few for private members to bring forward the ideas that their constituents often wish them to bring forward. To my mind the debate on the speech from the .throne offers an opportunity which is now seized by hon. members for that purpose.
I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) could expedite the business of the house if he would say whether it is the intention to move the various committee reports that were tabled on the last day of the last session. If it is not, then I shall object most strenuously to the suggestion that all the committees be set up -this week. With regard to radio and war expenditures particularly I am certain that some discussion should be undertaken in this house. If we have -the assurance that the reports are to be moved, then perhaps there would not be any need to enter into a debate when we are setting up the committees. But if we have not that assurance, members will naturally seize the opportunity-I know I myself intend to do so-when we are setting up the committees to discuss matters concerning radio and war expenditures. Other members may have other reports in their own minds.
As for -this house being a sounding board, I take it that this democratic institution affords the right to every member of parliament to bring forward matters which he considers of interest to his constituents and to the country. Therefore I object strenuously to any suggestion that the house is being used improperly as a sounding board.

I wish to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce another question. There are areas in Saskatchewan, and particularly in Alberta, where farmers have been unable to deliver practically any part of the 1943 crop because of the control of the allotment of cars. Hon. J. A. MacKINNON .(Minister of Trade and Commerce): The hon. member for Yorkton telephoned my office just before three o'clock and said that he intended to ask this question. I do not think the situation is quite as bad as his language would indicate, but undoubtedly transportation difficulties have prevented some producers from delivering as much grain as they wished to sell. Mr. -Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance, although I know, as the Prime Minister says, that he is a very busy man. I asked the minister a question on Monday last in regard to the slaughtering of animals by farmers in Quebec, and their being permitted to sell the carcass without a permit. I asked whether Ontario farmers and farmers in other provinces would have the same privilege.
Live Stock

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: NEW ARRANGEMENTS WITH REGARD TO SLAUGHTER OF ANIMALS BY QUEBEC FARMERS
speechtext:
I will give an answer to that now.
Briefly, the new arrangements may be described as follows. The wartime prices and trade board will issue slaughtering permits to local farmers' organizations in the province of Quebec, giving farmers who have registered with the local organization the right to slaughter their own live stock and to sell the resultant meat. The local farmers' organization will be responsible for the distribution and proper use of meat stamping equipment, for the completion of a monthly report by each registered farmer of slaughterings in relation to coupons collected, and for the preparation of a monthly consolidated report by the secretary of the local organization of total slaughterings by all registered farmers in relation to coupons collected.
These arrangements were recommended by and have the approval of the Quebec Department of Agriculture, whose field officials will cooperate with officials of the wartime prices and trade board.
The wartime prices and trade board is hopeful that the plan, which is not yet fully developed, will facilitate the slaughtering of live stock by individual farmers. As hon. members know, farm slaughtering has been almost universal in the province of Quebec, and it was particularly desirable to work out some method of issuing permits which would not interfere too greatly with established practice, while retaining the degree of control essential to the proper functioning of meat rationing. If the plan proves to be successful in the province of Quebec, the board will be prepared to extend the same arrangements to other areas in other provinces where similar conditions exist.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO LAY-OFF AT TORONTO SHIPBUILDING YARDS-PROCEDURE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO LAY-OFF AT TORONTO SHIPBUILDING YARDS-PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) asked a question regarding a reported lay-off by the Toronto Shipbuilding company. He wished to know what procedure was adopted in such cases, with special reference to returned soldiers.
The determination of lay-off procedure is the responsibility of national selective service, and since the question has been raised I should like to advise the house of the procedure which has been worked out as between national selective service, the Department of Munitions and Supply, and war contractors.

With the consent of the house I will do this; by placing on Hansard the following documents, which are self-explanatory:
1.	Circular of the Department of Labour, Employment Service and Unemployment Insurance branch, dealing with lay-offs in war and related industries.
2.	Circular issued by the Director of National Service with respect to lay-offs.
3.	Letter and circular signed by the deputy minister of the Department of Munitions and Supply which has been sent to all prime contractors to the Department of Munitions and Supply.
4.	Circular letter from the Acting Coordinator of Production of the Department of Munitions and Supply to all direetors-general of production branches, heads of divisions and presidents of government-owned crown companies, setting out the procedure which is to be followed in any changes involving stopping of production, reducing the rate of production or cancellation of orders.
The contents of these circulars will answer the question of my hon. friend and any other questions of this kind which may be asked during the session.
The procedure outlined affects lay-offs where the number of employees involved is in excess of fifty. The Department of Munitions and Supply does not ordinarily receive advice of any lay-off involving less than fifty persons.
In the case to which my hon. friend refers, I am advised that fifteen carpenters were given notice on Thursday, January 27. These men are no longer required because the specifications of the furniture and fittings on the particular vessel on which they were working have been changed from wood to steel.
I now table the documents:
Department of Labour Employment Service and Unemployment Insurance Branch Ottawa
December 27, 1943.
National Selective Service Circular No. 317
Subject: Lay-offs:-War and Related Industries
1.	This circular supersedes and cancels rulings and procedures Number E 10, dated January 23, 1943, and E 10A, dated March 31, 1943.
2.	The procedure outlined below will apply to all lay-offs, involving 50 or more persons, and due to the curtailing, cancelling or completing of orders for war and related materials but will not apply where the lay-off is d.ue to seasonal curtailment of civilian goods or services. Where less than 50 persons are involved the procedure outlined below will apply but notices and reports will not be required.
3.	Notifications of lay-offs will come from various sources, and generally head office will notify the regional office, which in turn, will
FEBRUARY 2, 1944	U7
Labour Conditions-Toronto Shipbuilding
notify the local office of the lay-off. On occasion, regional offices or local offices will be the first to receive a notice of lay-off; in these cases they will immediately notify the other offices; for instance, a local office hearing of a lay-off will advise its regional office, which, in turn, will notify head office, or if the regional office first hears of a lay-off, it will notify head office and the local office.
4.	When a lay-off is notified to a local 9ffice by a regional office, the latter office will issue instructions on the handling of the lay-off and advise whether a regional officer will advise on arrangements or whether the lay-off will be the sole responsibility of the local office. If a local office first hears of a lay-off it can assume that the lay-off will be its sole responsibility if the number of persons involved is less than 50 and it will immediately contact the employer and make the necessary arrangements, notifying the regional office by mail. If the lay-off involves 50 or more persons the local office will communicate with the regional office by wire or telephone and the regional office will then decide whether it will be necessary to send a regional representative to advise on the handling of the layoff, or whether this should be handled by the local office. The regional office will immediately notify the local office of its decision and issue any necessary instructions.
5.	It should be borne in mind that practically all lay-offs will be in industries covered by NSS Circular 282-A and B Labour Priority Industry

"Freeze" of employment, and consequently no person can be dismissed without the written permission of a selective servioe officer. This means that no lay-off can take place without the authorization of a selective service officer and further no lay-off is to be authorized until the procedures outlined ibelow are carried out.
6.	The officer detailed to communicate with the employer concerned will arrange for an orderly lay-off in the light of the general manpower situation at the particular time. He must courteously point out to the employer that we are definitely interested in who is, or who is not, to be laid off. It is not our intention that the least desirable or least efficient workers will be those to be laid off, but rather, first, those persons available for the army, and, second, other persons who can be moved to the advantage of, or with the least disturbance to the general labour situation. The demands for the army are continuing demands, and must have a definite priority, unless the persons available have exceptional skills which are greatly in demand by high priority industry, for example, tool makers, journeymen machinists, journeymen electricians, etc., should be transferred rather than be called up. The whole situation should be explained to the employer tactfully.
7.	In order to obtain men for the army the following procedures will be used:-
(a)	Where an Industrial Mobilization Survey has been completed the regional employment officer will direct an officer (preferably an investigator who has worked on the survey) to contact the employer, supplying him with a copy of the industrial mobilization survey plan, and the necessary subsidiary documents including Form NSS (M) 2-job description-for each man listed in the survey. He will -then be in a position to discuss the status of each employee on deferment. He should -advise the employer that up to the number involved in the lay-off, all men on deferment -according to the survey, will be called by the registrar, unless there are very good reasons for not ha%ring particular men
called. He should further advise the employer that, due to the reduction in production, there will probably be available some skilled men who were previously deemed to be very essential, but who could now be released. After carefully explaining the whole situation he should then go over the survey marking "A" against each man who can be called by the army (men over 38 years of age should not be included) and "T" against the name of each man available for transfer. Where a man is considered to be a key-man, the reasons for this consideration should be noted on the survey. If the number of available men on deferment is in excess of the number to be laid off, -the employer will be advised that those who are shown to be replaceable in the shorter periods will be called first and these men will be indicated on the survey. The employer will then be advised that those men will be called for army service, or for transfers and must be given notices of separation. It should be mentioned that a percentage of tbe men who are on deferment and who will be called by the military authorities, will not be accepted by them and may later be available for reemployment. If such men return to employment additional men on deferment, if available, must be given notices of separation. This procedure will in many cases look after an entire lay-off, but if the lay-off involves more people than can be taken care of in this manner the procedure outlined in paragraph 10 is to be followed.
(b)	Where no industrial mobilization survey has been made the officer on his first contact with the employer will request a list of all persons presently on deferment employed in the establishment, and a further list after the first one has been prepared of all other male persons in the designated age groups. These lists should be made up on form NSS (M) 1 -industrial mobilization survey and will be supplied by the officer and should contain all necessary information for the registrar to make calls. A similar procedure to that mentioned in (a) above will be followed for the first list, and an endeavour will be made to get as many men as possible for the army, and for transfer.
8.	The surveys and lists mentioned in paragraph 7 above will be sent immediately on completion to the chairman of the mobilization survey committee, in whose military district the lay-off occurs, for approval and submission to the divisional registrar. The registrar will thus be advised of the men available for the army and for transfer to high priority industry and will arrange to call up men and approve transfers. Transfers will be approved provisionally but local offices must mail to the registrar, a completed form 144-A-notice to divisional registrar (section C applies), marked "lay-off" in the upper right hand corner, for each individual who is transferred. The lists of men in the designated age groups but not on deferment will be supplied to the registrar by the chairman of the mobilization survey committee to assist in cheeking delinquents.
9.	When men on deferment are laid off and the registrar so notified, the local office^ tnust acquaint all placement officers who will be dealing with these men with this information. Men who have received, or will shortly receive their order-military training should only be referred to jobs of short duration and should not be referred to jobs of a permanent nature If it is decided by the registrar that certain men null not be called, the local office will be
8	COMMONS
Labour Conditions-Toronto Shipbuilding
so notified. Men who fail to pass the final medical examination, will be handled in the usual manner at the army reception centres.
10.	Where persons in addition to those on deferment are to be laid off, they should generally be laid off in the following order, subject, of course, to seniority rights where plants are covered by collective bargaining agreements, or subject to the conditions of any other employer-labour contracts:
(a)	Workers with previous agricultural experience, particularly dairy farm or stock raising. These persons will be directed, if possible, to year-round farm jobs;
(b)	Workers who are needed in other essential industries in the same vicinity;
(c)	Workers who are required by outside essential industries, and may be moved;
(d)	Younger -workers without family obligations (workers in this group are more adaptable, and are generally more easily moved).
(e)	Married women, if their husbands are supporting them.
(f)	Older men and women, if the foregoing classes have been exhausted.
It should be noted that generally women should not be laid off as long as they can replace men. Local situations may, however, alter this general rule, and discretion must be exercised.
11.	Employers should be requested to prepare nominal rolls on forms NSS 240A and 240B lay-off report-nominal roll, in triplicate covering all persons to be laid off. Samples of these forms are attached, and will be supplied by the regional office to local offices as required. When this nominal roll is completed by the employer, one copy will be left with him and the other copies will be used by the local office as the basic record for the lay-off. Complete instructions as to its use are on the back of the form.
12.	When persons are interviewed, forms U.I.C. 701 will be given the number shown on the lay-off report, nominal roll, for purposes of identification, and the name of the firm will be noted prominently on the 701. 701's for each separate lay-off will be kept in a separate file until final disposal of the applicant1 is made. If disposal of any person has not been made during the period of three weeks from the date of separation, the situation at that time will be considered to be final, and will be shown under the appropriate heading, and the 701 placed in the regular files. In other words, final disposition of all persons from lay-offs must be made in three weeks from the date of their separation. Otherwise, for record purposes, they are treated as ordinary applicants.
13.	Additional reports form NSS 240D, lav-off summary report, and form NSS 240C, lav-off summary weekly report, as per samples attached, will be prepared from the lav-off report- nominal roll. Form NSS 240D' will be completed at the close of the week following the week during which the first separation took place. Form NSS 240C will be completed for each subsequent week and will give the cumulative or to date totals for the lay-off. The final report, marked "final" in red ink. will be the report for the third week after the week of the last separation. This will allow sufficient time to record the disposition of the persons laid off and will not unduly prolong the period for

which reports are required. These reports -will be made in quadruplicate; two copies for head office, employment service division (one of these will be forwarded to the Department of Munitions and Supply). One copy for the regional office and one copy for local office files.
14.	The regional employment officer shall notify the regional insurance officer of any probable lay-off of fifty or more employees, unless the persons to be laid off can ,be placed immediately in other employment.
15.	Wherever possible, arrangements should be made to interview the workers who are to be laid off during the period covered by the notice of separation, and at the plant. Direct referrals to new jobs -will be made when possible, and the required permits issued. By interviewing at the plant, it is believed that situations will be handled in a much more orderly manner, that crowding and congestion at our offices will be avoided and that the workers and the companies involved will appreciate our efforts to offer new employment with as little lost time and inconvenience as possible.
16.	Lay-offs are difficult situations from every point of view, and all officers are cautioned to use courtesy, tact, and diplomacy in dealing with all parties concerned.
17.	This circular is effective January 3, 1944, and all lay-offs on and after that date must be handled as outlined above.
IS. Form NSiS 240-0, lay-off summary report

must also be completed, insofar as it is possible for all lay-offs which have taken place in the period from November 1. 1943, to December 31, 1943. Where a lay-off is in progress at December 31, 1943, a report will Ibe submitted as above, and then the procedures outlined in this circular *will be followed insofar as it is possible.
H. F. Caloren Allan M. Mitchell Director of Employment Service and Unemployment Insurance
(Letter attached to National Selective Service circular No. 317-1. January 19, 1944, Subject: Lay-offs-War Contractors.)
Information for War Contractors in Connection with "Lay-offs"
You are no doubt already aware that essential changes in Canada's war production programme necessitate certain "lay-offs". National Selective Service is most anxious in such cases to reassign employees promptly and with the least inconvenience to all concerned.
Definite instructions have been given to all offices of National Selective Service to cooperate fully with employers and to follow the procedure which is briefly outlined herein.
As you know, your establishment has been classified as a "designated establishment" under National Selective Service Civilian Regulations and consequently you may not terminate the employment of any male employee without the permission in writing of a selective service officer. Therefore, the closest nossible cooperation will be necessary in working out arrangements between yourselves and the local employment and selective service office.
Before giving any general or individual notice you are therefore required to discuss the matter

Labour Conditions-Toronto Shipbuilding
with the manager of your nearest employment and selective service office. He will be ready to render immediate assistance in working out the details of the "lay-off".
The procedure to ibe followed in reassigning labour due to "lay-offs" will be as follows:
1.	Owing to the needs of the army for a large number of men each month, the first step must be to release those men suitable for the armed forces. If an industrial mobilization survey has been completed for your establishment a representative of selective service will provide you with a copy of the survey plan and discuss with you the status of each employee on deferment with a view to making arrangements with the divisional registrar to call up such men for military training, unless there is very good reason why such men should not be called at this time. If no industrial mobilization survey has been made, you will be asked by the national selective service officer to provide a list of all persons in your employ presently on deferment, also a list showing all other male employees within the age groups and of the marital status designated under mobilization regulations.
2.	The next step to be taken should be to reduce working hours to 48 hours per week, or to the normal working hours per week for the industry if less than 48.
_ 3. Where it is necessary to lay off persons in addition to those on deferment, it is the intention that they should be laid off generally in the following order, subject of course to seniority rights where an establishment is covered by a collective bargaining agreement, or subject to the conditions of any other employer-employee contract:
(a)	Workers with agricultural experience, particularly in dairy farming or stock raising.
(lb) Workers whose services could be utilized in other essential industries in the vicinity of your establishment.
(c)	Workers whose services could be utilized by outside essential industries and who could be moved to such.
(d)	Younger workers without family obligations.
(e)	Married women if their husbands are supporting them.
(f)	Older men and women if the foregoing classes have been exhausted.
4. Wherever possible arrangements will ibe made to have national selective service officers interview at the plant the workers who are to be laid off and direct referrals to new jobs will be made when possible. This will enable national selective service to handle the situation in a more orderly manner and to offer new employment with as little lost time and inconvenience as possible.
Your cooperation in assisting our officers in dealing with this difficult situation will be much appreciated.
A. MaeNamara,
Director of National Selective Service

February 1, 1944.
To Prime Contractors to the
Department of Munitions and Supply.
Re: Procedure by prime contractors when instructions are received to stop production, to reduce the rate of production of stores or to cancel certain outstanding orders.
The pattern of this war is constantly changing and the demands made on this department and on Canadian contractors will likewise change.
These changed demands will necessitate the issuance, from time to time, of instructions to curtail production on certain stores and to stop production entirely on others. Some lay-offs of labour will doubtless result from such instructions.
If and when such an event odcurs, prime contractors are called upon to take certain steps which are outlined in the attached memorandum from the Director of National Selective Service, and in my letter of instruction, also attached.
The careful observance of these instructions will enable the government to make full use of the machinery which it has set up to ensure that Canada makes the best use of all available manpower.
This communication is not to be regarded as an indication that we think the war is over. It is to be looked upon purely as a preparation for changes in war demands. Such changes and the cancellations and adjustments which follow them are a part of the business of waging *war-not a sign that the war is over.
Will you please acknowledge receipt of these instructions.
G. K. Sheils,
Deputy Minister.

Department of Munitions and Supply.
Re: Pre-layoff procedure to be adopted by contractors to this department, immediately definite instructions are received either to stop production or to reduce production rates, or when outstanding orders are reduced-if any of the above acts will result in an immediate or subsequent layoff of labour.
When any one of the above conditions occurs you are requested to take the following action:
(a)	Communicate immediately with the local selective service officer as no lay-off may take place without that officer's consent,
(b)	Supply the selective service officer with the names and addresses of all sub-contractors affected by the production change,

(c)	Advise the above noted sub-contractors and suppliers and request them to communicate with their local selective service officer if layoffs are to occur,
(d)	Consult with your labour-management committee or the plant representatives of your employees before notices of separation are given and advise them, as far as is consistent with security-, of the reasons for the production change and ask them to inform the other employees.
Please note that, except in so far as necessary to carry out the above instructions, any and all advices regarding production changes are confidential as between this Department and your company.
No publicity must therefore be given to the said instructions or advices without the specific knowledge and consent of the department. If, in your opinion, some publicity is desirable and would be in the public interest, you will please submit your detailed proposals with respect thereto to the director general of the publicity branch of the department who will discuss the same with all parties concerned, including the censors, and will advise you if and when and to what extent these proposals are approved. If the matter should appear to you to be urgent, the publicity branch may be consulted bytelephone or telegraph.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the preliminaries to the carrying on of this debate have no doubt been most interesting to those who have been participating, but I can say they are very disconcerting to a member who is trying to rise in his place in order to proceed with the discussion. However, I am not complaining about that; I recognize that within certain limitations these privileges and rights are extended to hon. members.
In rising to take part in this, what has sometimes been called a time-honoured debate, sometimes characterized as a useless debate, I desire to make one or two observations. There is no doubt about it that in days gone by this debate on the speech from the throne has been carried on at altogether too great length. On the other hand, I would deprecate the wiping out in their entirety of the facilities that this debate offers. There is a happy medium; and in view of the announcement which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made yesterday, that the speech from the throne does not mean an election, I am hopeful that this debate will be concluded
within a reasonable time. I suppose it is all very well for me to say that when I am through and let the other fellow think he cannot speak at all. But there is no doubt about it, in my view at all events, that the debate on the speech from the throne serves a very useful purpose, and particularly at this time. Notwithstanding the clamour in certain portions of the press for the abrogation of this debate, I should like to point out that this house.has had a recess of at least six months, that during that period of time events of great importance and moment have occurred, that we have had no opportunity to review these events, and that it is difficult to do so when one is dealing with particular proposals by way of legislation. So that I say to you, sir, and to the membership of this house, that the debate on the address affords a very useful occasion to review events which have occurred in the long recess period of six months.
It is said that parliament is the great sounding board of the nation. That I think is true. Many of us have no other sounding board. We do not control the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, like the government does; we are not allowed to go on the air when we should like to do so. We may be able, if we have the money to buy the time and place, to go on the air and talk to our constituents, but we are subject to a strict censorship. I protest . against that, and I hope that this position will be reviewed at a very early date and that there will be freedom of the air as to-day there is freedom of speech in this house and a free public press. The situation with regard to the use of the facilities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is intolerable and it cannot be allowed to stand. The sooner it is reviewed by those in authority, the better.
I come to a consideration of some of the topics which are immediately before this house and the country. I am glad to see that my colleague, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) to-day invited the government to introduce at once the measures visualized in the speech from the throne so that we may have full opportunity of examination and analysis and express our approval or disapproval. The speech of His Excellency, put in his mouth by my right hon. friend and his colleagues, covers an imposing and extensive field. I should say that stress was laid on the transitional period and on the post-war period and the problems relating thereto rather than upon the immediate objective of the nation, the winning of the war.

If any proof of that fact is required it will be found in the events of last summer when the by-elections were held, by-elections which, if the administration had the confidence of the country, should in all cases have resulted in the return of government nominees; but which to the surprise and astonishment of myself, at least, resulted, in a series of crushing defeats for hon. gentlemen opposite. These by-elections indicated a lack of confidence in the administration. Some people will gloat over this defeat of the government, but to me it has brought very serious implications. I am not gloating over these defeats. In fact I may say very frankly to Your Honour and to the members of this house that I was rather appalled at the results of the by-elections.

When you witness in a rock-ribbed Liberal constituency such as Cartier the election of a gentleman who is, according to all the remarks that I have heard, an out-and-out communist then I say

that is something to think about. I know the gentleman's name is Rose, but that which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet. Can anyone say after that result in Cartier and after that result in Stanstead that this country is united? What happened in Stanstead? There was the triumph over a Liberal candidate of a candidate of the Bloc Populaire, a party with a purely nationalistic appeal. What does that mean? It means, if it means anything, disunity in this country and it is a deplorable state of affairs. In my judgment these results indicate that Canada is more disunited than it has been at any time in our history. The results axe quite clear. They are very discernible. They are the natural results which have flowed from the policies of the administration in the prosecution of the war. I do not propose to-day to traverse ground that I have covered on previous occasions. I make that assertion. I desire only to emphasize the fact that, in my view at all events, this administration has lost the confidence of the country and I do not think there is any doubt about it.
On Monday the Prime Minister spoke in what I considered to be a chastened mood. I can understand that. It was in marked contrast with past performances. He had his mechanical majority behind him but he has learned the lesson of humility. That is a fine thing for a prime minister to learn. It is a fine attribute for a prime minister to have. I have tried to cultivate that attitude myself, I do not know with what success; but I think it is a fine attribute for any public man to have. The Prime Minister took occasion to say that he wanted no general election before the expiration of the lifetime of parliament in June, 1945; but he so hedged his position, as he always does, by two qualifications, that it is difficult to be certain of his position. The first qualification was that "situations" might arise which would make it impossible for the government to carry on with the authority it should have in time of war. The second qualification which is rather similar to the first was, that some question might arise which would make it absolutely necessary that an appeal be made to the country to settle the issue. He left the door wide open. Make no mistake about that. He always does. That is part of the political strategy for which he is so famous.

speechtext:
The Prime Minister left the door wide open, and I suggest to him that he could always find an excuse. Therefore do not take this promise of no election this year too seriously. I am going to give my opinion about the matter a little later, and I am very serious about what I think ought to be done. If I wanted to be cynical I would say that the Prime Minister was from one point of view well advised in making that declaration. I am thoroughly convinced his party would be defeated at the polls if an appeal were made now or in the immediate future. That is the political angle of this question.
There is another angle to it. Personally I do not wish to be swayed by the political angle. Mere party advantage or place or the prospect of power in the immediate future certainly make no appeal to me as an individual member of this house when there is a war on. I am much more concerned about another great principle and it is this: I believe that the holding of a general election at this time or in the immediate future would be a distinct detriment to the successful prosecution of the war. I am very honest in that conviction. From the very beginning of this gigantic struggle-and I am sure hon. members will bear me out in this-I have taken the position and I have rigidly adhered to it that the supreme objective of the Canadian people, the supreme objective of the membership of this house, irrespective of party, the supreme duty of each and every one of us no matter what our political proclivities, or our point of view may be, is the winning of this war, and all other considerations, party and otherwise, are subordinated to that supreme consideration.
I was very glad indeed to hear the Prime Minister in his speech on Monday last utter a grave note of warning^ and again to-day that not only is this war not won, but it is far from being won. In fact, may I emphasize what the Prime Minister has alluded to, that war on the European front is now entering upon its most critical stage. The allied nations have invaded Europe through Italy. Further invasions are contemplated. The most exacting and dangerous no doubt will be on the western front. If we are at all realistic we must know that in attacking frontally the fortress of Europe as now dominated by the German forces the allied nations are undertaking the most courageous and herculean task in all history. Look at the map of Europe; visualize it with me, if you will. Germany dominates over half the whole continent of Europe. She is in absolute possession of Norway, Denmark, the low countries of Holland and Belgium, the whole of France, the major part of Italy and the Balkan states, while her own territory remains inviolate save and except for the destruction of her cities and her production programme wrought by the magnificent work of the Royal Air Force, the gallant Royal Canadian Air Force, and the great and wonderful contribution of the air forces of our mighty ally the United States of America.
There is the position. To say that the war is nearly over is folly and a fallacy. Nothing could be further from the truth; nothing could be more dangerous than to believe anything of the sort. To hold that belief; to relax our efforts in any degree is to invite disaster. And to hold a general election in three or six months, with the prospect of blood and carnage almost unthought of, perhaps beyond the scope and measure of our imagination, I honestly believe would be a letting down of our determination, our morale and our will to support the men at the front, and we must never do that. That is my considered view. Others may differ, but I desire to maintain that position in this house, and I think the Prime Minister might well have taken that position in the speech from the throne. However, he has repaired that omission; and speaking for myself I am satisfied, much as I have deplored the fact that at a time of such great national and international undertakings we in Canada have conducted this war on a party rather than on a national basis.
May I pause here, Mr. Speaker, to express my regret, yea, my astonishment, at the position taken by my hon. friend the leader of the Bloc Populaire (Mr. Raymond) in his recent speech in this house in which, if I understood

Has the hon. gentleman forgotten those hectic days of May and June, 1940, after Dunkirk, when nothing stood between the enemy and this Canada of ours-which I agree we both love-but the might, the power, the courage and I would almost say the majesty of the British navy, together with the magnificent will and determination of the British people under the matchless, indomitable leadership of Churchill, who, along with the British people, the royal navy, the merchant navy and the workers of Britain offered only blood, sweat and tears, and who not only saved this continent from invasion but saved civilization itself? For, make no mistake about it, the resolution, the fortitude and the bravery of Churchill and the British people did just that. Have we no gratitude in our hearts and minds for that magnificent achievement? From that has grown, with the help first of Canada and the other major sister dominions and then with the heartening aid of the United States and the wonderful contribution of the Russian people, the promising position of to-day, when, if victory is not in sight, it is at least within striking distance. In those days Britain attained the moral leadership of the whole civilized world. Standing alone she earned that position, and at great cost and sacrifice; and we as Canadians, irrespective of our racial descent, should recognize that fact and be eternally thankful. And with all kindliness and in all sincerity I say to my hon. friend that no part of Canada was more vulnerable than his beloved part. No part of Canada should be more thankful than that part of our citizenry which my hon. friend claims to represent, the people of his own province.
In the short space of time allotted to one, Mr. Speaker-and I suppose in days to come even that time may be cut down-it is extremely difficult to cover any wide range of subjects, and I am not going to attempt to do so.

It will be recalled that last year the Prime Minister made a declaration of policy with respect to this question of civil aviation, and that the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) did likewise. We also had some observations on the subject in the committee on railways and shipping by the president of Trans-Canada Air Lines. I am not going to repeat what those declarations were; they are well known to all our membership and to the country generally. I do think, however, that at a very early date this whole position should be debated and reviewed. In the speech from the throne there was an omission, a very significant omission, of any reference to this great problem; it contained not a syllable about post-war civil aviation. My colleague the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) referred to' this omission in his address on Monday, at page 20 of Hansard, in these terms:
There is no single economic subject fraught with such important effects and ramifications of a world-wide character which is so vital to Canada as commercial aviation.
I agree with that statement. We have the Trans-Canada Air Lines. I am not here to-day to criticize the operations of that enterprise, which started from scratch and has done very good work. No one will deny, however, that the government has been a "sugar daddy" to Trans-Canada Air Lines. Somebody had to father it, and the government did so. Perhaps I may be excused for using the term "sugar daddy"; it is a pretty comprehensive term, and everyone knows what is meant. This was used in another connection; it is a bit of slang we have borrowed from across the boundary line. We find that Trans-Canada Air Lines is just a government monopoly. It is operated for the government under the form of a private undertaking. It is not subject to the control of this parlia^ ment. It is not subject-or at least only to a very limited extent-to the control of the board of transport commissioners. Control, in the first instance, is vested in the board of directors, who are the creatures of the government, and the real control of Trans-Canada Air Lines is vested in the Minister of Munitions and Supply. He is behind it. He kept his hand on that when he left the Department of Transport to go to the department which he now heads. I am not blaming him; having

But their policy certainly is to prevent any competition from development by private enterprise. I do not think there is any gainsaying that. We are supposed to have a free economy in this country, outside of war time. That may be a fallacy. We are subject to tremendous control at the present time, under the guise of war-some of which control is wholly unnecessary. The initiative, the freedom to operate privately sponsored air transport is cabined, cribbed, confined and put in a strait-jacket. Even in the air a limited field has been left open to private enterprise, and allotted by government policy. If any proof is required of that statement, I can give it now. Recently application was made on behalf of a private enterprise to establish an airways route between the cities of Saint John and Halifax in the maritime provinces. The application was refused, and in my judgment the refusal was without justifiable or reasonable cause. The field is not occupied, and present facilities on the main line of Trans-Canada Air Lines do not fill the need.

There appeared in the January isue of the Atlantic Monthly, which I have on my desk, an article entitled "The Future of Air Transport, A British View," written by Peter Masefield, who is described by the editor as the personal adviser to Lord Beaverbrook on civil aviation as it affects Great Britain. This article is in no sense official. But because of our knowledge of the author and his position, any views he may express must command respect and attention. I commend a thorough study of the article to the minister and his advisers, and to every thoughtful student of the subject of aviation. His opening sentence is fascinating, and I would ask permission to read it. These are his words:
Air transport, a child of peace reared in war, approaches maturity. Under the spur of war, flying has found its technical independence. It is free to start anew- in the peaceful skies of to-morrow, hound only by such artificial restrictions as the nations cloose to apply.
He visualizes three great problems. First, there is the problem of policy and diplomacy, and he tells us that it is important that these should be resolved only by international discussion conducted in a spirit of good will and cooperation. The second is the question of

operational problems, matters of subsidy, monopoly, national air routes, traffic, frequency of services and of control. The third covers the technical problems of construction and equipment, which are the least important.
Under the caption "operating policy" he states that general opinion in Britain favours regulated rivalry rather than uncontrolled competition in national and international air line operation. Mark these words, "Monopolies are not favoured or considered efficient." I suggest to the house that these words bear the impress of truth and logic as we know them. Nowhere does he suggest either government operation or monopoly.
Participation by shipping and railroad concerns will be welcomed so long as it promotes efficient commercial operation for the good of air transport in general. I have not the time to analyse his position further, but it is quite clear that he does not visualize government monopoly in Britain. Rather does he approach the solution from the point of view of regulated private enterprise. I think that is the position in the United States.
Recently the Minister of Munitions and Supply visited London with Mr. Symington, the president of Trans-Canada. I believe they sat in on the meetings of a special committee which was set up under Lord Beaverbrook to consider empire air relations and policy. The mover of the address, the 'hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Tremblay) has expressed his opposition to immigration, and be deserves to be congratulated. I shall go farther than he, however, and I shall add that so long as settlers have to endure hardship on uncleared lots-I do not mean all the settlers-on rocky land, so long as they have not been given the opportunity of securing lots which may be cultivated or old abandoned farms-and there are several-so long as workers in war plants have not obtained employment elsewhere-and there are some who are already out of work-so long as there is a single unemployed person, immigration cannot be considered and refugees, irrespective of their race, cannot be accepted.
I have heard the hon. member for Toronto Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) make an appeal in favour of Jewish refugees, the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Gillis) and finally the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Rose) take a similar stand. In 1932-33, I believe, Right Hon. R. B. Bennett had an amendment to the Immigration Act passed by this house, under which the government could accept farmers only or, at least, a large proportion of farmers.

Can we hope that the men who so strongly advocated autonomy, and even nationalism in time of peace, and ye.t showed their true imperialistic colours in wartime, can we hope that they will stand firm this time?

The hon. member for Cartier spoke of slums; that is the best part of his speech. To the building of houses he should have added, however, the destroying of slums so that those infected areas might not be used once again. Because, for countless reasons, such as unemployment and the resultant lack of money, as well as the greater facilities for reaching the work-shops, they will again be filled if they are left standing. They must immediately be levelled down. They have contaminated too many citizens, mothers and children; they deserve to be destroyed.
That is where governments are remiss in their duty, tolerating as they do such a situation in the larger cities. Within every great urban centre which is left to itself, through negligence, ignorance or carelessness, there are inevitably wretched and unruly people as well as radicals. Some one has said-I think it was a Spanish prelate-: "Give a pretext to hotheads and an illusion to the wretched and you shall have a revolution".
Having said that, I shall now discuss socialism.
In the first place, it is recognized and history shows that socialism has never transformed any country into a land of milk and honey. Socialism has risen, in all countries and especially in France,-it did its work underground long before that,-as an aftermath of revolution. Socialism was at that time converging from England, where Karl Marx was living, and from Central Europe, then included within Germany; it has fully blossomed forth in Russia with the Mensheviks and the Bolsheviks, the latter, more radical and daring than the former, have achieved the success which we all know.
They always resort to revolutions in order to usurp power. They have preached everywhere the equality of wealth, of the social classes while raising the latter against one another. Do not believe that these socialist leaders have remained poor. Jaures was a millionaire when he died. It was he who was going down into the coal mines, with a Bible under his arm, saying to the workers: "We must share our wealth. The rich must share with the poor." This is what prompted a French writer who had followed the evolution of socialism to write: "Once upon a time, there was a socialist who did not own a castle."
Lenin was by no means a poor man, and history tells us of the shady methods he resorted to in order to obtain funds for his propaganda. The socialists of Russia have for leader Stalin, the most crafty politician ever. It cannot be gainsaid that he has had the tact necessary to rouse the Russian people and to mould them into a warlike and well organized nation.
Those who believe that his decree abolishing the communist party in the world frees the nations from the menace of a world revolution must be very credulous indeed: the communist party has a new name, that is all there is to it. The cells have increased their activity due to relaxation of watchfulness on the part of statesmen and democracies. In our country, communism was declared illegal, but it has changed its name. Its old leaders head the Labour-Progressive party, however the name is different. This nefarious joke has lasted altogether too long and we shall fall victims to our credulity before long.
I read a small pamphlet written by the hon. member for Cartier, "La cinquieme colonne d'Hitler dans Quebec" (Hitler's Fifth Column in Quebec). It has a green cover and is fairly well printed. Some hon. members of this house are mentioned in it. I am not a socialist and, on the other side of this house, I see other members who, are not either. It may be that a few historical facts will refresh my hon. friend's (Mr. Rose) memory and prove to him that Hitler's fifth column is not recruited in the league for the defence of Canada nor in the Bloc Populaire Canadien, but elsewhere.
Barthou had, one day, succeeded in negotiating commercial agreements to the advantage of France. He was a Republican. He was assassinated as soon as he set foot on French soil. The man who defeated these treaties to Hitler's profit, a socialist named Bonnet, was convicted of espionage, with his wife, and was accused of this crime by all French wtiters. He was not a member of the Bloc Populaire Canadien. He was a member of Hitler's fifth column in France.
Enough said. I might be called a grumbler. Now, I come, at the end of my remarks, to the slogan coined by the Prime Minister, to the anathema uttered against the Bloc Populaire Canadien: the bloc, that is the enemy! It must be defeated in Quebec, or the party is lost. Not that way, though, not by stating that the Bloc Populaire is appealing to race prejudice. That was not swallowed in Stanstead, neither will be swallowed elsewhere in Quebec or in the other provinces where we shall have a certain number of candidates in the next federal election. In Stanstead-and

He has told us about Dunkirk where the British army fought so successfully to cover the evacuation and added that we French Canadians should thank England for having stopped Hitler's march at that time. Have we blamed England for protecting that evacuation? No.

But reverting to a subject dealt with by the former leader of the opposition, I would say that, had not the French Canadians been here, in 1775 and 1812, to hold the country for the British crown he would not have been in this house to make his utterances, this afternoon.
We do not forget easily, our memory is good, faithful and well exercised. We are little impressed by the anathema uttered against us. We have a programme, we intend to realize the union of French Canadians; we shall seek this end; we have the right to do so and whenever we have the opportunity to do so and we shall continue to work with that object in view. This is clear, very clear indeed. Attempts are made to spread all kinds of rumours on the Bloc Populaire. Some say that we are secessionists, that we aim to ostracize all races in Quebec first, and later in Canada as a whole and then to hound everybody out of Quebec and Canada. There will be other elections in which we shall have candidates who will fight for unity among our fellow-citizens even if we are accused of appealing to race prejudice, every time we demand that the rights and privileges justly belonging to us on- account of our numbers and our ethnical importance, be respected.
